newsitem.title: MALDIVES: India, Pakistan seek right ambience for peace.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan seek right ambience for peace.

text.p: The new leaders of India and Pakistan established a degree of trust at their first encounter that will be needed to help the neighbours overcome 50 years of acrimony, diplomats said on Tuesday.
But the path towards lasting peace will quickly lead towards divided Kashmir -- their most intractable dispute that lies at the heart of the two nations' rivalry, they said.
Both Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and his Pakistani counterpart, Nawaz Sharif, were upbeat after 90-minute talks on a resort island in the Maldives on Monday.
"Undoubtedly this is going to be a new chapter in our bilateral relations," Gujral told reporters late on Monday after the talks with Sharif had ended.
"We parted as the best of friends. Nawaz Sharif walked me to my cottage to say good-bye to me," Gujral said.
Gujral and Sharif spent 15 minutes alone on Monday before holding some 75 minutes of talks, with six close aides of each leader present.
Sharif told reporters he had a personal friendship with Gujral, who like him has roots in the Punjab region. "I like the man very much," Sharif said.
Diplomats said they spoke a mix of English and Urdu during their discussions. Gujral recited a couplet by the famous Urdu poet Faiz.

Sharif told Reuters Television on Tuesday: "I think the situation has taken a good turn. We have held talks yesterday after a deadlock of four years. The talks were very constructive, very meaningful, and we've agreed to talk more."
Diplomats on both sides who sat in on Monday's meeting said Sharif and Gujral appeared to have formed a personal bond.

"They were aware of each other as individuals, of their political careers, of what it signifies," said Indian Foreign Secretary Salman Haider, adding that the talks were marked by "humour and a human element".

A senior Pakistani diplomat who attended the talks told Reuters: "There was the right ambience. They seemed convinced of each other's sincerity and focused on a common need to settle their differences."
Sharif was named prime minister in February after general elections, while Gujral assumed power on April 19 after a three-week political crisis in India.

In Pakistan, a column in the English-language daily The News said the arrival in power of Sharif and Gujral was "a God-sent opportunity to the people of Pakistan and India to finally improve relations between the two countries.
"If we miss this chance, we may not get another one for years," it said.

In India, the Asian Age said in an editorial: "Mr Gujral has a 'nice guy' image. Mr Sharif is a hard-headed businessman by profession who brings to his politics a sense of pragmatism. Given the right amount of understanding and pragmatism, maybe there will be real advance in certain key areas."
A senior Pakistani diplomat, asked to name the biggest challenge for the two leaders, said: "Fifty years of history."
The two rivals have fought three wars in their half decade of independence, two of them over divided Kashmir.
The Himalayan region has been the biggest stumbling block to peace, and could remain so despite an agreement to establish working groups to tackle all outstanding issues.

Pakistani Foreign Secretary Shamshad Ahmed told reporters one of the groups would be devoted to Kashmir. But his Indian counterpart, Salman Haider, said the two had agreed only to set up working groups and not yet specified the subjects.

Pakistani Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan had tough words on Monday as he walked into the bilateral talks, saying India should reduce its security forces in Jammu and Kashmir state, which he said numbered 700,000.
"The army has more or less gone berserk in occupied Jammu and Kashmir," he said.
India says Pakistan's estimates of troop levels in Jammu and Kashmir are exaggerated, and perpetuators of human rights violations are prosecuted.
